column1: # Platform seam registry — the source of truth for what crosses the platform boundary.
# Why this file exists
# A "seam" is a type bound differently in PlatformModule.android.kt and PlatformModule.jvm.kt.
# The repository has 25 of them. Ten have a JVM implementation that is an inert stub — the
# binding resolves, the caller calls it, and nothing happens. Nothing fails, because a
# no-op that is bound looks exactly like a no-op that works.
# The static unwired-surface detector cannot see any of it: `orphan-binding` hard-filters to
# CoreDiModule.kt, and it reports only bindings nothing injects. A port that is bound,
# injected and called — but inert — is outside its model.
# Two Desktop bugs were live on origin/main because of this:
#   - a reminder was written to Room and no alarm was ever armed (JvmReminderScheduler)
#   - every sync push evaporated on sign-in (NoopSyncWorkScheduler)
# Both are now either fixed (sync) or made visible from the UI (reminders: the scheduler
# declares `isSupported = false` and callers refuse before persisting). Classifying a seam
# as `stub` therefore does not excuse a lying UI — the registry row is where that gets
# recorded, and the gate that enforces honesty lives next to the caller.
# So the registry classifies every seam, and PlatformSeamGuardTest fails when:
#   - a seam's named implementation disappears from a platform module
#   - a seam marked `real` is actually a Noop/NoOp/Stub
#   - a seam marked `stub` carries no written reason
#   - a seam declared `injected` is referenced NOWHERE outside its two bindings
#   - a NEW typed binding appears in a platform module with no registry row  ← the load-bearing one
# That last rule is the point: seam 26 cannot be added silently.
# The `injected` rule exists because of NotificationPort. It was bound on both
# platforms, looked real, and no production code injected it — while its JVM half
# shelled out to `atq`/`atrm` and deleted every `at` job on the host, jobs the
# user had queued outside the app. A binding that nothing calls is invisible to
# `find-unwired-surfaces.py`, which reports only bindings nothing injects *and*
# only within CoreDiModule.kt. So this registry says so out loud instead.
# Format: pipe-separated, `#` starts a comment, blank lines ignored.
# Columns: port | kind | androidImpl | jvmImpl | verdict | wiring | reason
#   kind    seam  — platform-divergent; impl names are asserted
#           infra — infrastructure binding (paths, DataStore, scope); presence only
#   verdict real    — the JVM implementation genuinely works
#           stub    — the JVM implementation does nothing; reason is REQUIRED
#           exempt  — inert by deliberate, documented choice; reason is REQUIRED
#           infra   — not a behavioural seam
#   androidImpl / jvmImpl — a distinctive token that must appear in that platform's module.
#                            `-` when the platform has no binding (declared Android-only).
# Adding a binding? Add a row here first. The gate will remind you if you do not.
SyncPeriodicTrigger|seam|AndroidSyncPeriodicTrigger|DelayLoopSyncPeriodicTrigger|real|injected|-|

GoogleSyncPeriodicTrigger|seam|AndroidGoogleSyncPeriodicTrigger|DelayLoopGoogleSyncPeriodicTrigger|real|injected|-|Google sync runs on both platforms, so both bindings are real: WorkManager on Android, a delay loop on Desktop. Listed separately from SyncPeriodicTrigger because they are two schedulers for two features, and a row each is what stops one of them being dropped from a platform module unnoticed.
SyncWorkScheduler|seam|AndroidSyncWorkScheduler|JvmSyncWorkScheduler|real|injected|-|

CalendarSyncWorkScheduler|seam|AndroidCalendarSyncWorkScheduler|NoopCalendarSyncWorkScheduler|stub|injected|isSupported|Calendar sync is Android-only by design. The port declares isSupported and the JVM answers false, and the panel's gate is the conjunction of the four calendar seams' flags - the provider, the settings repository, the app queries and this scheduler - so the Desktop settings UI is capability-gated and the scheduler cannot be mistaken for working.

ReminderScheduler|seam|AlarmManagerReminderScheduler|JvmReminderScheduler|real|injected|isSupported|Desktop arms one `systemd --user` transient timer per reminder and the unit runs this app's own launcher (`fire-reminder`), which reads the fresh task title from Room exactly as AlarmReceiver does. Still not the deleted at backend: cancellation is a targeted `systemctl stop` on a name we chose, never an enumeration. isSupported is now a conjunction of a systemd user session and a working notify-send, so a container or CI runner reports false instead of arming a timer nothing can display. The gate is the UI's reminder slot refusing before it persists a row.

CalendarSyncRepository|seam|CalendarSyncSettingsRepositoryImpl|NoopCalendarSyncRepositoryImpl|stub|injected|isSupported|Android-only feature. The port declares isSupported and the JVM answers false, so the toggle is not merely off — it cannot work here. The panel that offers it is gated by the conjunction of the four calendar seams' flags (the CalendarProviderPort row), and this is one of the four.

CalendarProviderPort|seam|AndroidCalendarProvider|NoopCalendarProvider|stub|injected|isSupported|Android-only feature. The port declares isSupported and the JVM answers false, and the panel's gate reads that flag — so the Desktop is told it needs Android instead of being offered a switch that does nothing. The Result.failure is no longer the signal.

CalendarAppQueries|seam|AndroidCalendarAppQueries|JvmCalendarAppQueries|stub|injected|isSupported|Android-only feature. The port declares isSupported and the JVM answers false, and the ViewModel asks the port before listing — so the empty list it used to return is no longer presented as "you have no calendar apps", it is the port saying it cannot do its job here. The port's flag is one of the four the panel's gate is the conjunction of (the CalendarProviderPort row).

PomodoroTaskListProvider|seam|AndroidPomodoroTaskListProvider|JvmPomodoroTaskListProvider|stub|injected|isSupported|Desktop returns an empty, never-updating list, which was indistinguishable from an empty Inbox. PomodoroScreen.kt now reads isSupported and says the picker is unavailable here instead of showing no chips. Fixes the same defect class as the reminder gate.

PomodoroScheduler|seam|PomodoroAlarmScheduler|-|exempt|injected|-|UNGATED but harmless: Desktop drives the pomodoro timer in-process via PomodoroTimer (registered separately as real), so no UI offers to schedule a desktop alarm that will not happen.
BackupCodec|seam|AndroidBackupCodec|JvmBackupCodec|real|injected|-|
SecureStoragePort|seam|AndroidSecureStorage|JvmSecureStorage|real|injected|-|
FileSystem|seam|AndroidFileSystem|JvmFileSystem|real|injected|-|
HostEnvironmentPort|seam|AndroidHostEnvironment|JvmHostEnvironment|real|injected|-|
FileRevealer|seam|AndroidFileRevealer|JvmFileRevealer|real|injected|-|
FileSourceFactory|seam|AndroidFileSourceFactory|JvmFileSourceFactory|real|injected|-|
SharePort|seam|AndroidSharePort|JvmSharePort|real|injected|-|
FileSharePort|seam|AndroidFileSharePort|JvmFileSharePort|real|injected|-|

FileOpener|seam|AndroidFileOpener|JvmFileOpener|real|injected|-|Gated by OpenOutcome rather than by isSupported: the caller has no UI decision point to gate on, because "can this device open a PDF" is not a static capability of the platform, it is a property of what the user has installed. Both implementations return NoHandler rather than throwing, and AttachmentViewerHost turns that into a screen offering the share sheet. Android's extra SecurityException arm (no app holds the FileProvider grant) maps to the same outcome as ActivityNotFoundException on purpose: the user-visible situation is identical — this file cannot be opened here.
PomodoroTimer|seam|AndroidPomodoroTimer|JvmPomodoroTimer|real|injected|-|

Haptic|seam|AndroidHaptic|createHaptic|exempt|injected|-|UNGATED by necessity: a definition must exist on every platform or composition fails. The task detail composes haptics unconditionally, so there is no UI decision point at which a capability could be checked — the Desktop implementation is simply inert.

CrashReportingPort|seam|FileCrashReportingPort|JvmCrashReportingPort|exempt|injected|-|UNGATED by necessity: Desktop logs through loggingBackgroundFailureHandler. Crash reporting has no user-facing control to gate, so a capability flag would have nothing to protect.
# ── Infrastructure bindings: present on both platforms, not behavioural seams ──────────

Notifier|seam|AndroidNotifier|JvmNotifier|real|injected|isSupported|Replaces the deleted NotificationPort, which is NOT to be revived: its JVM half used at(1) and cancelled every at job on the host. This port can only display something — it has no way to enumerate or cancel system units, so the original failure has no code path here. JvmNotifier probes notify-send at runtime rather than asserting a constant, so a headless host reports false.
AppDatabase|infra|-|-|infra|injected|-|
DataStore|infra|-|-|infra|injected|-|
BackgroundWorkScheduler|seam|AndroidBackgroundWorkScheduler|JvmBackgroundWorkScheduler|real|injected|-|
CoroutineScope|infra|-|-|infra|injected|-|
String|infra|-|-|infra|injected|-|

UnitOfWork|infra|-|-|infra|injected|-|RoomUnitOfWork on both platforms, so not a seam: it is Room's own withWriteTransaction and the Android and Desktop databases are the same type. Bound in both platform modules because both need the transaction, and listed here because a binding that appears in a platform module with no row is exactly what this file exists to make impossible. See ADR 2026-10-05-who-owns-a-row-and-the-patch-that-describes-it.

ToolCallLog|seam|AndroidFileToolCallLog|JvmFileToolCallLog|real|injected|-|The tool-call records are written by a different implementation on each platform, because the platforms differ in what they can offer: the JVM writer names its file after the process id and restricts it to the owner, the Android writer uses a random token and writes into the app's private storage, which the platform already keeps away from other applications. Both are real: the records land in the application's own data directory, and a write that fails never reaches the caller.

OAuthBrowser|seam|-|JvmOAuthBrowser|real|injected|-|The browser is opened only on the desktop. The Android sign-in goes through Google's own authorization API — Play Services carries the answer back — so there is no browser and no loopback socket to open on Android. Google blocked the loopback flow for Android clients in October 2022, so a browser-based sign-in there would fail against Google's own rules.

OAuthRedirectSocket|seam|-|JvmOAuthRedirectSocket|real|injected|-|The loopback socket exists only on the desktop, for the same reason as the browser: a Desktop OAuth client may use the loopback redirect, an Android one may not. It is bound in the platform module rather than constructed in the consent, so the platform piece has one owner.

GoogleGrantRevoker|seam|SupabaseGoogleGrantRevoker|LocalGoogleGrantRevoker|real|injected|-|Where the grant is revoked follows from where the refresh token lives: on Android it is on the server, so the server cancels it there — the row is deleted and the token is revoked at Google in one request — while on the desktop it is in the device's own keystore and Google's revoke endpoint needs no client secret, so there is nothing for a server to do. Same reasoning as the redeemer row, and the same split.

GoogleGrantRedeemer|seam|SupabaseGoogleGrantRedeemer|LocalGoogleGrantRedeemer|real|injected|-|Where the grant is redeemed is the platform's business, and the two differ for a reason: Google's offline flow gives the app a one-time code that only a holder of the client secret can redeem, and a client secret inside an APK is a secret that has leaked — so Android redeems on the server and the desktop redeems on the device, where a Desktop client is a public client and needs no secret.

GoogleAccessTokenProvider|seam|SupabaseGoogleAccessTokenProvider|LocalGoogleAccessTokenProvider|real|injected|-|Who renews the access token follows from where the refresh token lives: on the server on Android, in the device's own keystore on the desktop. An access token lasts about an hour and the sync runs unattended, so the renewal has to happen somewhere that can renew it — and a caller that read the store directly would have to know which of the two it is on.
